chapter_theme: At the Ganga the Chera Senguttuvan has the pathini's stone bathed, rewards his warriors, and hears from the Brahmin Maadalan the aftermath of Madurai: Madari's fire, Kavunthi's fast, the renunciations and deaths of the parents, Madhavi's taking of robes, the new Pandya's offering of a thousand goldsmiths and the soundness of the Chola sceptre; then he rewards the Brahmin, sends the captives away and returns to Vanchi as the songs of hill, field, pasture and shore announce him.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanchi who brought the pathini's stone from the Himalaya and bathed it in the Ganga (named here also குடவர் கோ, பொறையன், வில்லவன், வானவன்)
the Brahmin of Puhar (மாடல மறையோன்) who brings the Chera king news of what followed Kovalan's death
Kanaka and Vijaya, the northern (Arya) princes who defied the Tamil king and were made to carry the stone on their crowns
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
Kovalan's wife, the pathini whose stone the Chera has brought
the dancer-courtesan of Puhar with whom Kovalan lived
the old herdswoman of Madurai in whose house Kannaki was lodged
the Jain nun who went with the couple to Madurai
Kovalan's father, a great merchant of Puhar (named here கோவலன் தாதை)
Kovalan's mother (named here துறந்தோன் மனைவி)
Kannaki's father, a great merchant of Puhar (named here கண்ணகி தாதை)
Kannaki's mother, the wife of the merchant who gave gifts
Madhavi's mother
Madhavi's daughter by Kovalan
the young Chola king, the Chera's cousin (மைத்துனன்), whose rule nine kings would not bear
the nine kings of one mind who rose against the young Chola
the Pandya of Korkai who took the throne of Madurai after the king's death
the Chera king's astrologer, who reckons the time since the army left Vanchi
the northern kings taken captive in the campaign
the thousand chamberlains (cloaked officers) sent to show the captives to the other two kings
the Chera king's chief queen, waiting in Vanchi
the queen's nurses of her retinue
the hunchbacked and dwarf attendants of the women's quarters
the hill women who sing on the millet-watch platform
the ploughmen of the Chera land, who sing to their oxen
the cowherds of the Porunai ford, who play the flute
the girls of the shore who play kazhangu with pearls and sing the vanji

silappathikaram:27:1-17.reading: The narrator recounts that, after the stone for the goddess-pathini had been taken from the Himalaya and set on the crowns of Kanaka and Vijaya, the Chera, whose army had reckoned its slaughter of the northern kings who fought him not knowing Tamil strength, came with his host to the bank of the Ganga and had the pathini deity bathed by men learned in the rite.
silappathikaram:27:1-17.nuance: The kaathai is named for this bathing (நீர்ப்படை), told in a single subordinate clause (lines 15 to 16) before the poem turns to the camp; the rite is done by நூற்றிறன் மாக்கள, men who know the treatise, not by the king. The pathini is called கடவுட் பத்தினி and பத்தினிக் கடவுள், a goddess, before any temple is built. Lines 7 to 12, where the work of the old death-dealer swells and the army reckons years, months, days and hours, and the eighteen (ஒன்பதிற்று இரட்டி) and the one day's span are given, are compressed and the count is not clear.
silappathikaram:27:1-17.event: Senguttuvan, the northern kings beaten in a day's battle, reaches the Ganga and has the pathini's stone bathed there.

silappathikaram:27:18-42.reading: The king enters the camp on the open ground of the Ganga's south bank, in halls, pavilions, groves and pools that the Arya kings had built for him, and the narrator lists the warriors he will honour: those who broke enemy kings' hearts and were wed like brides of the gods, those who lay with head and shoulders paid for in battle, those who died with their swords as the hollow-eyed demoness sang their praise in her kuravai, those who wore the victor's garland and stood red with their wounds.
silappathikaram:27:18-42.nuance: The list puts the dead and the living in one catalogue: the dead are given the heavenly marriage (வானவர் மகளிரின் வதுவை) and a demoness's praise, the living are marked by wounds, and all are the same grammatical subject of the honours given in the next lines. The Arya kings' building of the camp for the conqueror (line 22) is tribute, not hospitality.
silappathikaram:27:18-42.unit_note: The boundary between the second and third units was moved from after line 33 to after line 42. Line 33 broke a phrase (கிளர்பூண் ஆகத்து / வளையோர் மடிய); line 42 ends with மறவர், the head noun of the whole list of warriors, and line 43 begins the king's giving.
silappathikaram:27:18-42.event: Senguttuvan enters the camp the Arya kings built for him on the Ganga's south bank.

silappathikaram:27:43-56.reading: Calling his wounded warriors forward, the king gives them golden vaagai leaves through the long festival hour, and as he sits in state, crowned with palmyra and thumbai, the Brahmin Maadalan appears and hails him, saying that Madhavi's seaside song crushed the crowned heads of Kanaka and Vijaya, and the king asks what this jest, unknown to the kings of the enemy lands, means.
silappathikaram:27:43-56.nuance: Maadalan's riddle makes a courtesan's song the first cause of a northern war: the kaanal vari split Kovalan from Madhavi, which led to Madurai, to Kannaki, and to the stone the northern kings now carry. The king calls it நகைத்திறம், a jest, and asks for its sense; the next units are the answer.
silappathikaram:27:43-56.unit_note: The unit begins at line 43, where the boundary was moved from after line 33 (see the previous unit); it ends where the given unit ended, at line 56.
silappathikaram:27:43-56.event: Senguttuvan rewards his warriors, and Maadalan arrives and tells him Madhavi's song crushed the crowns of Kanaka and Vijaya.

silappathikaram:27:57-77.reading: Maadalan explains that at the sea-play on the cool shore, in a time of sulking, with Madhavi's vari song, the deed of the past rose in wrath, Kovalan left her and went with his wife to Madurai, was killed, and his wife came into the Chera's land and rose onto the crowns of the northern kings; then he tells why he came: returning from circling Pothiyil and bathing at Kumari, by karma's fruit perhaps he went to Madurai, heard that the woman had beaten the king with her anklet, and saw Madari rise in the common and cry that Kovalan was blameless, the king had erred, and she had lost the one put in her keeping.
silappathikaram:27:57-77.nuance: Line 59 gives two causes in one breath: the lovers' sulk (ஊடற் காலத்து) and the deed of the past rising (ஊழ்வினை உருத்தெழ). Maadalan then puts even his own arrival at Madurai under karma, as a question (ஊழ்வினைப் பயன்கொல்), while Madari blames the king outright (கோமகன் பிழைத்தான், line 75) and her own failure to guard her charge. So the unit sets karma, the king's fault and a guardian's failure side by side without choosing among them. Madari's அடைக்கலம் is a ward entrusted to her, not a devotee's refuge at a god's feet.
silappathikaram:27:57-77.event: Maadalan tells Senguttuvan how Kovalan left Madhavi, died in Madurai, and how Madari cried out that the king had erred.

claims.claim: the deed of a former birth rose in wrath and parted Kovalan from Madhavi
Kovalan was without fault and the king erred in killing him
one who loses a person given into her keeping has failed in her trust

silappathikaram:27:78-95.reading: Maadalan goes on: Madari entered the fire in the middle of the night; Kavunthi, the ascetic, in her anger at the king, asking whether the couple's deed had risen against her too, gave up her life by the vow of not eating; having learned all that befell Madurai he went home to Puhar and told it, and Kovalan's father, hearing what came to his son, his son's wife and the king, gave away great wealth, entered the seven Indra viharas and renounced before the three hundred sky-walkers who strive to end the birth of the body.
silappathikaram:27:78-95.nuance: Kavunthi's question (line 82) is the striking thing: a Jain nun, who has taught that deeds come back to their doers, asks whether the couple's deed has come back on her, the one who led them, and answers with the fasting death. Lines 80 to 81, with the king's departing life and the patient woman, are hard to construe: whether the king's death is the time of her fast, or what she could not bear, is not clear. Kovalan's father renounces at the Indra viharas, which the poem placed in Puhar under the five-branched bodhi (Silappathikaram 10), so his renunciation is in the Buddhist order; the unit does not state the doctrine, only the aim of ending birth.
silappathikaram:27:78-95.event: Madari enters the fire, Kavunthi fasts to death, and Kovalan's father, told by Maadalan, gives away his wealth and becomes a renouncer.

claims.claim: the deed of those one has guided may rise against oneself
renouncers strive to end the rebirth of the born body

silappathikaram:27:96-115.reading: Maadalan says that Kovalan's mother, unable to bear her son's grief, died; Kannaki's father gave gifts before the Ajivika ascetics in their godlike guise and took their dharma, and his wife died too; and Madhavi, hearing it, told her mother that Manimekalai must never see the courtesan's guise that brings great sorrow, cut off her hair with its garland and took dharma with a gift at the bodhi; since those who heard the news from his mouth died, he has come to bathe in the Ganga; and the king asks what the Pandya land has done since its king died.
silappathikaram:27:96-115.nuance: The same news ends in renunciation for the two fathers and Madhavi and in death for the two mothers. The two merchants turn to different orders, Kovalan's father to the Indra viharas, Kannaki's father to the Ajivikas (ஆசீவகர், line 99), and Madhavi to the bodhi (போதித் தானம், line 108); the poem names the orders without ranking them. Madhavi's reason is her daughter: she renounces so that Manimekalai will not take up the courtesan's life, the thread the Manimekalai follows. Maadalan bathes in the Ganga because his telling caused deaths (line 109), a messenger's guilt for the news he carried.
silappathikaram:27:96-115.event: Kovalan's mother and Kannaki's mother die of grief, Kannaki's father joins the Ajivikas, and Madhavi cuts her hair and renounces; Senguttuvan asks about the Pandya land.

claims.claim: the courtesan's guise brings great sorrow to the daughter who takes it up
one whose words have brought death to others should cleanse himself in the Ganga

silappathikaram:27:116-137.reading: Maadalan answers by first praising the king, who, when nine kings of one mind would not bear the young rule of his cousin the Chola Killi, destroyed their nine umbrellas in a single day, and who felled the neem guarded by Pazhaiyan, and then tells that Vetrivel Cheliyan of Korkai, in one day, fed the lives of a thousand goldsmiths as an offering to the pathini who cut off one breast, and, when Madurai had lost its king in its time of distress, mounted the throne of justice as the morning sun mounts the god's chariot.
silappathikaram:27:116-137.nuance: The new Pandya's first act is an offering of lives (உயிர்ப்பலி) to the pathini: the craft of the one goldsmith who lied is punished a thousandfold, and the poem gives it as worship, not as a sentence. The unit does not say the goldsmiths were guilty. Maadalan's praise of the Chera for the Chola succession shows the three crowned houses bound by kinship: the Chera intervenes for a cousin of his mother's line.
silappathikaram:27:116-137.event: Maadalan tells how Vetrivel Cheliyan offered a thousand goldsmiths to the pathini and took the Pandya throne.

silappathikaram:27:138-161.reading: Maadalan ends that the heir of the moon's line has ascended to guard the world age after age, and as the king sits listening, evening falls, the sky reddens and the white crescent shows; the astrologer rises and tells him thirty-two months have passed since he left Vanchi; the king goes back through the streets of the camp to his hall, has Maadalan called by the gatekeepers and asks whether, since the young princes died, the Chola's rule and its sceptre are still sound.
silappathikaram:27:138-161.nuance: The sun-and-moon image of lines 137 to 138 turns the Pandya succession into a change of lights: the line descended from the moon goes on as the sun goes down. The astrologer's count of thirty-two months reminds the king, and the reader, how long the vow for the stone has kept him from home. Who the young princes (இளங்கோ வேந்தர், line 159) were is not said in the unit.
silappathikaram:27:138-161.event: At evening the astrologer tells Senguttuvan he has been away thirty-two months, and the king asks Maadalan about the Chola's rule.

silappathikaram:27:162-172.reading: Maadalan answers that the victory of the Chola line, who destroyed the three forts the gods marvelled at, and the dharma-giving sceptre of the one who cut his own body to end the little dove's distress and the hawk's hunger, can never turn; there is no fault, even in a time of trouble, with the lord of the land the Kaveri guards.
silappathikaram:27:162-172.nuance: The assurance rests on lineage: the sceptre cannot bend because of what an ancestor did. The dove story, which Kannaki threw at the Pandya as a reproach, is here a guarantee offered to a Chera about a Chola. The answer is given as a rhetorical question (திரிந்துவேறு ஆகுங் காலமும் உண்டோ), not as a report of how the Chola has ruled.

claims.claim: the just sceptre of a line whose ancestor gave his flesh for a dove cannot bend, even in hard times

silappathikaram:27:173-187.reading: The king honours the Brahmin and gives him gold to fifty times his own weight, sends the hundred Arya kings back toward their lands, and with them the princes of great armies who saved their lives in ascetics' guise, the Arya pedis with curled beards, flower-hair, long eyes, bangles and anklets, and the chamberlains who refuse the commands of the defiant kings.
silappathikaram:27:173-187.nuance: The gold is measured against the king's own weight (தன்னிறை), the giver's body as the unit of the gift. The princes who escaped in ascetic guise (தாபத வேடம்) are a jibe: the renouncer's garb worn as a disguise to live. The pedis are described with a mix of male and female marks (a beard with a woman's eyes, bangles and breasts); what their role was is not said. Whether all these groups go home with the hundred kings or are sent elsewhere, and how ஐயிரு பதின்மர் and ஆடகப் பெருநிறை ஐயைந்து இரட்டி are to be counted, is not certain; the sentence runs on into the next unit.
silappathikaram:27:173-187.event: Senguttuvan gives Maadalan gold of fifty times his weight and sends the captive Arya kings away.

silappathikaram:27:188-203.reading: The king sends a thousand chamberlains to show Kanaka and Vijaya, who fought not knowing Tamil strength, to the two other great kings, and before he has slept, as the young sun rises over the eastern hills and bees hum in the Ganga's lotus fields, the western king, wearing the northern thumbai and vaagai, turns south with his army toward his treasure-filled city.
silappathikaram:27:188-203.nuance: Showing the captives to the Chola and the Pandya makes the northern victory a message to the other two Tamil crowns; the Tamil strength the northerners did not know (அருந்தமிழ் ஆற்றல், line 189) is the same phrase as the kaathai's opening (line 5), so the campaign is framed as Tamil against Arya. From line 200 the unit has already moved to the queen's palace in Vanchi.
silappathikaram:27:188-203.event: Senguttuvan sends Kanaka and Vijaya to be shown to the Chola and Pandya kings and sets out south for Vanchi.

silappathikaram:27:204-224.reading: In Vanchi, the queen lies sleepless on a golden bed of swan-down in her gem-set hall; the nurses who know the king's chariot victories sing that her grief at parting will end and wish her long life; the hunchbacks and dwarfs come to tell her that her lord has come and her hair should take its festival adornment; and the hill women on the watch platform sing their kurinji song, telling the wild elephant that came to eat the millet while the toddy-drunk watchman dropped his sling to leave the path of the king's war elephant.
silappathikaram:27:204-224.nuance: The return is told through the queen's waiting and the voices that reach her: first those of the palace, then the hill women. The kurinji song turns its own landscape's scene (the elephant raiding the millet) into news of the king, so that each region's song, here and in the next units, bends to the same refrain that he has come. The queen's sleep is ambiguous: துயிலாற்றுப் படுத்து suggests she was laid to sleep, while the nurses sing to end her grief.
silappathikaram:27:204-224.event: The queen's nurses and attendants announce the king's coming, and the hill women sing of it in their kurinji song.

silappathikaram:27:225-239.reading: The ploughmen sing their own song, that the lord of the west, the ploughman who yoked donkeys and sowed kavadi on the ruined forts of the northern kings, has come, that tomorrow the oxen will not wear the yoke, and that this is the white festival that frees kings from their fetters; and at the Porunai ford, bright with the colours, powders and flowers the bathers left, the cowherd boys perched on a thazhai branch call that Villavan has come back from the Himalaya and the herds should be taken to the water.
silappathikaram:27:225-239.nuance: The ploughmen's title for the king, the donkey-plough ploughman of the enemy's forts, is a war rite (ploughing a ruined fort and sowing it with worthless seed) that the field-workers sing as their own; the same song gives their oxen a holiday. The white festival that frees kings' fetters (line 229) seems to be a release of captives at the king's return, but the line is brief and its sense not sure.
silappathikaram:27:225-239.event: The ploughmen and the cowherds of the Porunai sing that the king has come.

silappathikaram:27:240-256.reading: The cowherds play their flute as the king's herds bathe at the ford, the girls of the shore lift pearls born of the right-whorled conch in their bangled hands for the kazhangu game and sing that Vanavan has come and they will sing the vanji with thumbai and palmyra; the queen listens to all these songs, and the king, under the white umbrella, crowned with vaagai and high on his swift elephant, is met by the city with a train of elephants and enters Vanchi.
silappathikaram:27:240-256.nuance: The four songs, of hill, field, pasture and shore, make the four landscapes of the Chera land greet one king, and the queen hears them all (line 251) before she sees him. The kaathai ends with the king's name (செங்குட்டுவன்), as the stone, the bathing and the news of Madurai give way to the triumph.
silappathikaram:27:240-256.event: Senguttuvan, met by the city with elephants, enters Vanchi while the shore girls sing and the queen listens.

links.note: The decade's preface lists among Senguttuvan's deeds that he sought the stone of the goddess-pathini (கடவுள் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள்) and bathed in the Ganga; the epic opens this kaathai with the same phrase and the same river.
links.teaches: Set beside the preface, the epic's நீர்ப்படை is seen to rest on a Chera tradition that already called the pathini a goddess and joined her stone to the Ganga, and the epic's contribution is the story that makes her one: who she was and why a king would march north for her.

gains.a: the bathing gains outside witness: a Chera praise tradition that names the pathini's stone among the king's conquests
gains.b: the bare line of the preface gains the woman behind the title and the reason the stone was wanted

links.note: Maadalan says Madhavi's seaside song crushed the crowns of Kanaka and Vijaya; the earlier unit is the moment she takes up the yazh in a sulk to answer Kovalan's songs.
links.teaches: The scene of a lovers' misreading of each other's songs on the beach turns out, in Maadalan's riddle, to be the first link in a chain that ends in a northern war, so the poem asks the reader to see a small private quarrel and a campaign as one sequence of cause.

links.note: Kannaki told the Pandya that Kovalan came to Madurai driven by former deeds; here Madari cries that Kovalan was blameless and the king erred, and Maadalan puts the parting under karma.
links.teaches: Kannaki in her plea names both karma and the king's failure to inquire, and this report splits those causes between witnesses, the Brahmin naming karma and the herdswoman naming the king, so the epic keeps both explanations alive in the story's aftermath rather than letting either replace the other.

links.note: The patikam promises that the deed of the past comes in wrath to be eaten and that the great praise a pathini; Maadalan uses the same verb (ஊழ்வினை உருத்தெழ) and says the woman has risen onto the crowns of the northern kings.
links.teaches: The patikam's morals are fulfilled here in a messenger's words: the praise of the high is made literal as kings carrying her stone on their crowns, and the wrathful deed is placed at a courtesan's song, a smaller and more human moment than the former-birth curse the patikam gives as its cause.

links.note: The Charana taught Kavunthi that the strong deed comes back to face its doer; here she asks whether the couple's deed has risen against her too and dies by fasting.
links.teaches: The doctrine she heard says a deed returns to its own doer, but the nun who led the couple treats their deed as falling on her as their guide, so the epic shows a Jain ascetic acting on a shared responsibility that the Charana's rule of individual return does not name.

links.note: Both tell a death by refusing food: the Chera Perunjeralathan, ashamed of a wound in his back, sits facing north with his sword; Kavunthi, after the deaths of her wards, gives up life by the vow of not eating.
links.teaches: The fasting death that the Sangam poem shows as a warrior king's answer to shame is in the epic taken up by a Jain nun as an answer to failed guardianship, so the same act carries the honour code into the renouncer's vow.

gains.a: Kavunthi's brief death gains a Tamil precedent that makes it read as an answer to dishonour, not only as grief
gains.b: the king's death gains a counterpart outside the warrior class, showing the act could be chosen by a renouncer for a failure of care rather than of valour

links.note: The quatrain says the best renounce home and wealth after slowly seeing that nothing lasts; here Kannaki's father and Madhavi renounce on hearing of deaths, and the two mothers simply die of the same news.
links.teaches: The quatrain's renunciation comes from calm reflection on impermanence, while in the epic it comes from the shock of bereavement and is only one of two outcomes of the same grief, so the pair shows the distance between the ethics book's ideal path to renunciation and the way the story's people actually reach it.

gains.a: the epic's renunciations gain a standard by which they look sudden and grief-driven rather than reasoned
gains.b: the quatrain's ideal gains a case showing that the same knowledge of loss can end in death as well as in renouncing

links.note: The preface says Senguttuvan, son of the Chola Manakkilli, felled Pazhaiyan's neem and made nine heirs of the Chola house fall at the gate; Maadalan praises him for destroying the nine umbrellas that would not bear his cousin Killi's young rule and for felling Pazhaiyan's neem.
links.teaches: Read together, the preface's nine Chola kin felled at the gate are given a cause in the epic, a war over the succession of a young Chola who was the Chera's cousin through his Chola mother, so the Sangam list of victories becomes a family quarrel among the crowned houses.

gains.a: Maadalan's allusions gain the record of the same deeds and of the Chola mother that explains the word மைத்துனன்
gains.b: the preface's bare list gains a reason for the war on the nine and a sense of why a Chera would fight in Chola affairs

links.note: The couplet likens a king's killing of the cruel to weeding the crop; the new Pandya kills a thousand goldsmiths in one day as an offering of lives to the pathini.
links.teaches: The couplet's punishment by death is of the cruel, one by one, as care for the crop, while the epic's new king kills a whole craft for one goldsmith's lie and calls it an offering, so the pair shows royal punishment sliding from justice into collective sacrifice to restore a king's standing.

gains.a: Cheliyan's act gains a measure from the ethics of the sceptre against which its scale and its form as offering stand out
gains.b: the couplet gains a case that asks who counts as the weed when a king must atone for a predecessor's wrong

links.note: Both recite the Chola line's ancestors, the king who entered the scale for the dove and the one who destroyed the hanging fort; the puram poem praises a Chola who withered the Chera's unwithering Vanchi, the epic has a Brahmin recite the same lineage in the Chera's own court.
links.teaches: The praise of the dove-king's line, which in the Sangam poem celebrates a Chola's victory over Vanchi, is spoken in the epic before the king of Vanchi as a pledge that the Chola's sceptre is sound, so the formula once used against the Chera now serves an alliance between cousins.

gains.a: Maadalan's assurance gains its source: a fixed Chola praise in which the dove, the fort and the just sceptre go together
gains.b: the puram formula gains a later use in which the rival it once mocked hears it as reassurance

links.note: Kannaki threw the Chola who relieved the bird's distress at the Pandya as a reproach; Maadalan offers the same ancestor to the Chera as proof that the Chola sceptre cannot bend.
links.teaches: The one exemplum works in two directions within the epic, as an accusation of a king who failed and as a guarantee for a king who has not been tested, which shows how the ancestor's deed stands in for an inquiry into the living king's justice.

links.note: The Chola of the puram poem entered the scale with his own body to save a dove from a hawk; the Chera here gives the Brahmin gold measured against his own weight fifty times over, just after the Brahmin has praised that very dove-king.
links.teaches: The scale in which a Chola ancestor weighed his flesh against a bird becomes in the Chera's court a scale in which the king's weight is matched in gold for a messenger, so the body-as-measure moves from self-sacrifice to royal gift.

gains.a: the weighing gains the Tamil memory of the royal scale, which makes the gift an answer to Maadalan's praise of the dove-king
gains.b: the dove story gains a later royal practice in which the king's body is weighed for giving, not for suffering

links.note: The bard of the puram poem hails Athiyaman as the ploughman who yokes white-mouthed donkeys on the bloody fields of captured forts and sows white varagu and horse-gram; the Chera's ploughmen sing their king as the donkey-plough ploughman who sowed kavadi on the northern kings' forts.
links.teaches: The terror title that a Sangam bard gives a patron at his gate is in the epic sung by real ploughmen in their field song, beside their oxen's holiday, so the conqueror's mock ploughing of enemy ground is absorbed into the farming folk's festival of his return.

gains.a: the ploughmen's epithet gains the rite behind it: ploughing a ruined fort with donkeys and sowing it with poor seed
gains.b: the bard's title gains a later setting where the king's own ploughmen own it as a song of joy

links.note: When the Chera Perunjeralathan sits north to die, the ploughmen's cry is forgotten and the village festival forgotten; when Senguttuvan returns, the ploughmen's song and the bathing festival fill the land.
links.teaches: Holding the two Chera poems together shows the ploughmen's song as the land's own measure of its king, silenced by a king's shameful death and loud at a king's triumph, so the epic's return scene answers the Sangam lament with its exact reverse.

gains.a: the field songs gain a Sangam frame in which the ploughmen's voice is a sign of the king's fortune
gains.b: the lament gains its opposite case, showing what the forgotten songs were when the king lived and won

source_issues: The kaathai header gives a printed last line of 255 against 256 lines held; the count differs by one somewhere in the kaathai.
Line 135 reads நிரைமணிப் புரவி ஓரழ் பூண்ட; ஓரழ் is not a word and is probably a corruption of ஓரேழ் (the sun's seven horses).
Line 188 spells ஈரைஞ் ஞூற்றூவர் where line 128 has ஈரைஞ் ஞூற்றுவர்; one of the two is a misprint.
Lines 7 to 12 (the reckoning of the slaughter by years, months, days and hours, and the number ஒன்பதிற்று இரட்டி) are compressed and may be damaged; the count cannot be fixed from the text.
The given boundary after line 33 broke a phrase; units 18-33 and 34-56 were re-cut as 18-42 and 43-56.
